message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What You’re Generally Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|-----------------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit, two months for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a written receipt.
• Request a written itemized list of deductions if you disagree. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a safe, livable condition (plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity).
• Must comply with all building, health, and safety codes. | • Notify landlord in writing (email or letter) of needed repairs.
• If repairs are not made within a reasonable time, you may withhold rent or repair & deduct (see below). | | **Repair & Deduct / Rent Withholding** | • If landlord fails to fix major problems, you may:
 1. Pay for the repair yourself and deduct the cost from rent (up to $500).
 2. Withhold rent until repairs are done (but only if the issue is material and you give notice). | • Keep receipts and document the problem.
• Provide written notice to landlord before withholding. | | **Privacy / Entry** | • Landlord must give at least 24 hours written notice before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Lease Termination** | • If you break the lease early, you may be liable for rent until the landlord re‑rents the unit, unless the landlord can prove they found a new tenant quickly.
• Landlord must provide a written notice of termination (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month). | • Review your lease for specific clauses. | | **Rent Increases** | • For month‑to‑month leases, landlords must give 30 days’ written notice before raising rent.
• For fixed‑term leases, rent can’t be increased until the lease expires. | • Ask for a written notice of any increase. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must serve a written notice (usually 3 days for nonpayment, 30 days for lease violation).
• Eviction must go through court; you have the right to contest. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• Attend any court hearing. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must provide water, sewer, and garbage removal.
• Other utilities (electric, gas, internet) are typically tenant responsibilities unless otherwise stated. | • Verify utility responsibilities in your lease. | | **Maintenance of Common Areas** | • Landlord must keep common areas clean and safe. | • Report issues in writing. | | **Right to a Written Lease** | • While not required by Texas law, having a written lease protects both parties. | • Request a written lease if you’re signing a new agreement. | ### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Look for clauses on security deposits, repairs, entry, and termination. 2. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of emails, texts, and written notices. 3. **Know the Notice Periods** – 24 hrs for entry, 30 days for rent increases, 30 days for lease termination. 4. **Report Problems Promptly** – Give written notice for repairs; follow up if not addressed. 5. **Keep Receipts** – For any repairs you pay for yourself. 6. **Know Your Local Resources** – Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs, local tenant‑rights groups, and the Texas Commission on Human Rights. --- #### When to Seek Legal Help - **Disputes over security deposit** that you believe are unjustified. - **Repeated or serious habitability violations** that the landlord ignores. - **Potential discrimination** in housing. - **Complex lease terms** or large financial obligations. You can also contact the Texas Attorney General’s Office or local legal aid organizations for free or low‑cost assistance.
